record.title: Authors report unified likelihood-based training with accuracy, coverage and retention tradeoffs
record.summary: A 67-page preprint frames pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning and suitable reinforcement-learning updates as likelihood fitting over a time-varying mixture of static data and successful model-generated targets. Its shared objective and trainer allow those sources to overlap; conventional staged training is a special case. The authors report controlled 124M-parameter reasoning-puzzle experiments and heterogeneous-data experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model. They report better accuracy, coverage, retention or continual-learning outcomes in several evaluated settings, alongside task and schedule tradeoffs. The paper explicitly describes the results as small-scale and does not establish predictive scaling laws or a universally preferred data mixture.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors posted a 67-page preprint on 29 October 2026 describing a likelihood-based framework that represents pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning and suitable reinforcement-learning updates as fitting a mixture of data-source distributions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In controlled experiments with a 124M-parameter model and reasoning puzzles, the authors report settings where unified training improves accuracy, coverage or generalization under matched training-compute comparisons, while other evaluated settings favor staged training on some metrics.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In heterogeneous-data experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model, the authors report retention benefits and a stronger starting point for subsequent coding reinforcement learning in tested mixtures, with tradeoffs across accuracy and coverage.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish independent reproduction, a predictive scaling law, a universally preferred data mixture, or transfer of its measured effects to frontier-scale models and varied multi-task training regimes.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent implementation or reproduction of the paper's controlled or heterogeneous-data results was found in this review.
The paper's experiments cover 124M and 0.76B models and mainly one RL task at a time; scaling behavior and joint multi-task transfer remain unestablished.
The paper does not identify a generally optimal mixture or schedule, and does not establish a predictive method for selecting mixtures from model/task properties.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported data-mixture and continual-learning gains transfer across model scales and tasks, a shared likelihood objective could change how teams allocate training data and compute across pretraining and post-training. The score reflects that potential program-level consequence; experiments remain author-reported on 124M and 0.76B models with no independent reproduction or predictive scaling law.
limitations: All numerical outcomes in this record are author-reported; no independent reproduction or code artifact was inspected.

The controlled study uses a 124M-parameter model and synthetic verifiable reasoning puzzles; the separate heterogeneous-data study uses a 0.76B-parameter model. Neither establishes transfer to frontier-scale models.

The paper explicitly describes its empirical scope as small-scale, does not establish predictive scaling laws or a universally preferred mixture, and reports tradeoffs among accuracy, coverage and retention.
Most runs optimize a single RL task at a time. The results do not establish joint multi-task training behavior or advantages over long sequences of subsequent tasks.
brief.summary: A 67-page preprint frames pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning and suitable reinforcement-learning updates as likelihood fitting over a time-varying mixture of static data and successful model-generated targets. Its shared objective and trainer allow those sources to overlap; conventional staged training is a special case. The authors report controlled 124M-parameter reasoning-puzzle experiments and heterogeneous-data experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model. They report better accuracy, coverage, retention or continual-learning outcomes in several evaluated settings, alongside task and schedule tradeoffs. The paper explicitly describes the results as small-scale and does not establish predictive scaling laws or a universally preferred data mixture.

technical.claimed_result: For a controlled 124M-parameter model trained on 20B pretraining tokens and a 510M-token reasoning-puzzle corpus, the authors report that selected unified mixtures improve accuracy or coverage against selected staged baselines at several compute budgets and retain more general benchmark performance than staged midtraining. In separate experiments with a 0.76B-parameter model and heterogeneous web, math, code and reasoning data, they report improved retention and better downstream coding RL for tested mixtures, with accuracy/coverage tradeoffs.
technical.compute_or_cost: The controlled study uses a 20B-token pretraining run plus a fixed 510M-token midtraining corpus and reports compute-frontier comparisons including pretraining, midtraining and RL generation/training. The 0.76B study uses a 240M-token heterogeneous corpus. No general cost-saving or frontier-scale compute claim is established.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv record and full paper provide inspectable mathematical definitions, trainer description, experimental protocols and result tables. The paper publication and what its authors report are established; the numerical training outcomes have not been independently reproduced in this review.
technical.implementation_status: A shared data format, loss and asynchronous trainer are described in the paper. No public implementation repository was identified in this review.
technical.mechanism: The paper represents each static or generated source with a prompt and target distribution, assigns time-varying mixture weights, and applies one maximum-likelihood loss to their mixture. Suitable reinforcement-learning objectives are recast as fitting success-conditioned model outputs; changing the data distribution and mixture schedule changes what is learned while the loss rule remains the same. Its practical trainer mixes static records and generated RL examples in a shared asynchronous data buffer.
technical.novelty: The paper's contribution is a common likelihood formulation and trainer for static data and suitable RL-generated targets, making data mixture and schedule the shared control variables. It builds on MaxRL and related likelihood views of reinforcement learning; it does not claim that likelihood training or offline/online data mixing are wholly new.
technical.regime: Author-run 124M-parameter controlled reasoning-puzzle experiments and 0.76B-parameter experiments with Math12K and a 240M-token heterogeneous midtraining corpus. Main controlled RL outcomes average two training seeds. Evaluation includes synthetic verifiable reasoning puzzles, math/coding benchmarks and held-out retention measures. The paper calls its evidence small-scale; most runs optimize one RL task at a time.
technical.reproducibility: The full paper exposes methods, configurations, tables and appendices. This review found no linked public code or independent reproduction. The authors themselves identify scale, mixture selection, longer task sequences and task interactions as open work.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within the controlled experiment, staged training uses the same pretraining and midtraining sources, MaxRL objective, RL-update budgets and evaluation tasks; authors select the staged initialization by its final RL accuracy. Compute-frontier comparisons allow the best observed checkpoint under each total budget. In the heterogeneous experiment, staged and unified runs start from the described base model and use the same subsequent coding RL configuration; the paper includes an asynchronous-trainer 0% mixing ablation.

brief.title: Authors report unified likelihood-based training with accuracy, coverage and retention tradeoffs
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported results transfer across tasks and model scales, teams could treat data allocation across pretraining and post-training as one coupled design problem instead of selecting separate training algorithms for each stage. The evidence supports a potentially useful training framework and measured small-scale tradeoffs, not a general replacement recipe for frontier-model training.
